title: The Cipher of the DMZ
premise: Kestrel Iversen, a crash investigator who lost her parents and sister in an unexplained accident over the DMZ, has built a career making disasters disappear into plausible causes. When a North Korean defector named Min-jun arrives claiming her father once saved his life—a debt Kestrel never knew existed—he brings a cipher recovered from the wreckage that proves row twelve was no accident. Pursued by the intelligence service that ordered the shootdown and by the man who executed it, Kestrel must decode her father's final message, which names the surviving official who can expose the truth. In the end, she trades the cipher itself—her family's last secret—to smuggle Min-jun and twelve other defectors across the border, choosing found family over vengeance, though she keeps one page back as insurance against the man who killed them.
about_author: Jude Eastwick is a former aviation safety consultant who spent a decade writing incident reports before turning to fiction, drawn to the stories reports could never tell. Eastwick lives near a decommissioned airfield and writes at dawn, when the fog makes runways look like unfinished sentences.

chapters.title: Row Twelve
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Opening on the anniversary of the crash, Kestrel closes out another 'attributed' investigation, erasing uncomfortable truths for a client. She visits the memorial wall where her family's names sit in row twelve of the victim list. Emotional beat: grief worn smooth into professional numbness.

chapters.title: The Favor That Never Was
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A stranger, Min-jun, intercepts her outside her office, insisting her father saved his life in 2003 and that a debt is owed—with interest. He leaves a battered metal case before vanishing. Inside: fragments from the crash site that should not exist. Beat: the floor drops out of her controlled world.

chapters.title: Fragments
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Forensic examination shows the wreckage pieces carry shrapnel patterns inconsistent with any published cause. Her father's handwriting appears on a hidden lining: a partial cipher keyed to something called PHEASANT. Beat: dread curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: The Man Who Watches Airports
chapters.summary: Introduce antagonist POV: Callum Reeve, a retired intelligence officer who executed the DMZ operation decades ago, learns the case file has been touched. He begins quietly pulling threads toward Kestrel. Beat: cold, patient menace; the hunter wakes.

chapters.title: Min-jun
chapters.summary: Min-jun's POV. Flashback to his defection and the night Kestrel's father, a UN flight inspector, hid him aboard a cargo plane. He explains why he waited twenty years: the cipher was useless until someone with Kestrel's access could finish it. Beat: guilt and devotion entwined.

chapters.title: Attribution Denied
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She pulls the original crash dossier through old contacts and finds pages redacted in a way only one agency redacts. Her supervisor warns her off with unusual urgency. Beat: the machinery of silence closing around her.

chapters.title: Pheasant
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Kestrel and Min-jun decode the first layer: PHEASANT was a covert overflight program, and row twelve carried a witness who could have ended it. Reeve's team burns a safehouse they'd traced. Beat: the past becomes actively lethal.

chapters.title: Twelve Names
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The cipher lists twelve people still alive who were part of the operation—including, impossibly, Kestrel's godfather, Daniel Voss, who helped raise her after the crash. Beat: betrayal as vertigo; love and duty begin their war.

chapters.title: Voss
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Confronted at his lakeside cottage, Voss admits he falsified the report to protect Kestrel from becoming a target—and because he believed the mission protected thousands. He gives her one name above his own. Beat: a father-figure's confession, half absolution, half trap.

chapters.title: Interest Owed
chapters.summary: Min-jun's POV. Reeve's operatives capture Min-jun's handler in Seoul, forcing Min-jun to choose between fleeing and standing by Kestrel. He stays. Their partnership deepens into something unspoken. Beat: loyalty crystallizing into love neither will name yet.

chapters.title: The Second Key
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The cipher needs a second key held in a decommissioned airbase archive—the same base her father flew from. Kestrel and Min-jun infiltrate it during a storm. Beat: breathless tension; first real act of rebellion together.

chapters.title: What the Fog Remembers
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Inside the archive they find her father's full letter: he knew the mission would kill him if he spoke, so he encoded everything and trusted his daughter's profession to find it. Reeve's team nearly corners them; they escape through the fog. Beat: inheritance redefined—not property, but purpose.

chapters.title: Collateral
chapters.summary: Reeve's POV. Reeve, pressured by the still-living senior official, orders Kestrel's death staged as an accident—an ugly mirror of row twelve. Voss intercepts the order and burns it, sealing his own fate. Beat: the antagonist's banality; the protector's sacrifice set in motion.

chapters.title: The Lake House Burns
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel arrives to find Voss dead and the cottage torched, staged as suicide. Grief breaks her numbness open. Among the ashes: Voss's own copy of the cipher page naming the top official—General Aldous Wren. Beat: rage with direction.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Now a decorated statesman, Wren meets Reeve and orders the problem solved completely—Kestrel, Min-jun, the cipher, all of it. We see his self-justification: order over truth. Beat: the true scale of the enemy revealed.

chapters.title: Trade Secret
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Cornered, Kestrel realizes the cipher is the only currency valuable enough to buy what she needs: passage for Min-jun's twelve stranded contacts still hiding along the border. She proposes the trade to a journalist with intelligence ties. Beat: the terrible arithmetic of sacrifice begins.

chapters.title: The Journalist's Price
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The journalist, Ada Okonkwo, agrees—but wants publication, not burial, meaning exposure before extraction. Reeve feeds Wren false assurance while quietly planning to take the cipher for himself. Beat: shifting alliances; trust as a knife held edge-up.

chapters.title: Demilitarized
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Min-jun's POV. The extraction night: twelve defectors move through the DMZ corridor under cover of a joint inspection exercise Kestrel engineered using her investigator credentials. Reeve's team closes in. Beat: peak tension; every thread converging on the wire.

chapters.title: The Wire
chapters.summary: Climax, dual POV. At the border fence, Reeve confronts Kestrel personally. Min-jun takes a bullet shielding her; she trades the cipher case to Reeve at gunpoint to get the wounded across—knowing she kept the decisive page hidden in her coat. Reeve lets them go, believing he holds everything. Beat: love against duty resolved in blood and choice.

chapters.title: Publication
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Okonkwo publishes using the page Kestrel withheld plus Voss's recovered testimony. Wren falls; Reeve, exposed as the executor, disappears rather than face trial. Beat: justice arriving incomplete but real.

chapters.title: Insurance
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Recovering, Kestrel reads her father's decoded letter in full—his apology, his hope that she would spend the truth well rather than hoard it. She files the last page in a bank vault, addressed to whoever comes asking next. Beat: mourning transmuted into stewardship.

chapters.title: Found
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Min-jun's POV, closing. Months later, Kestrel runs a small independent investigative practice; Min-jun, healed, teaches her Hangul over bad coffee. The twelve defectors send New Year photos. On the memorial wall, she adds nothing—but she finally stops visiting alone. Beat: quiet resolution; family chosen, grief carried lightly at last.
